utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you call the case, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody, and we start with the usual routine. Is there anything wrong, Mr. Brdjanin? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not have a translation. THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is everything okay? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning. Everything is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are understanding me, I presume, in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And General Talic, can you hear me in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. My name is Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor. If I can introduce you this morning to Nicholas Koumjian who will be leading the next witness, and our case manager today is Ms. Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome. Appearances for the Defence of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with my co-counsel Milka Maglov and legal assistant Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for General Talic. MR. De ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. de Roux, I'm assisted by Natasha Fauveau and Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. de Roux, last week, as you already know, we did not have the pleasure of your presence and that of your co-counsel Mr. Pitron. It is unfortunate that this Chamber was not given an explanation for your absence, something that we would have expected as a matter of courtesy, apart from the fact that we all agree here that you owe an explanation in any case. The same applies to Mr. Pitron, of course. But what is of more concern to this Trial Chamber is that when it sought the -- not exactly the consent but the advice of your client to see what was his reaction to the fact that his lead counsel and co-counsel were not present in the courtroom, he informed the Trial Chamber that he himself had not been made aware of the reasons for your absence. This Trial Chamber has no doubt that you had a very valid reason, both of you, for being absent from this Chamber, but also you have responsibilities under the brief that you have been trusted with by this Tribunal, and I would suppose that you have some sort of explanation to give to this Trial Chamber now. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to accept my apologies for this incident, but I would like to remind you that first of all, I personally was kept in Paris for a certain number of medical check-ups, which will happen again. Mr. Pitron was kept at the Court in Aix-en-Provence. He was involved in a very important case which relates to something that exploded, and this had been set a long time ago, and, obviously, he was not able to avoid this. But I would like to say the Defence wasn't absent since Ms. Fauveau was present for the Defence. Natasha Fauveau -- Ms. Natasha Fauveau is well acquainted with the situation. She knows the case very well, and I would say that she knows it in greatest detail, because first of all, she has been working full time on it for over two years now; and secondly, she sees this case not only in its translated versions but in the original, in her original language, because she speaks this language fluently, Serbo-Croat. It's her mother tongue. So she can read the dossiers, the cases in the originals, and pay attention to all the details. I think that Defence counsel was present and present in a very efficient manner for General Talic during the hearings of last week. And I don't think that the Defence counsel has failed in any way. Now, I would like to remind you that I was first appointed by General Talic. I defended him until July, until last July and I was assigned by the Tribunal. I intend to provide the best possible defence to General Talic within the limits of the budget that the Tribunal has allocated to me, and I really think that Defence has not failed for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. de Roux, the abilities and capacities of your colleague, Ms. Fauveau, in defending General Talic are not in dispute. What is in dispute is her role as one of General Talic's official counsel here. She is not on record one of his counsel. You are the lead counsel that has been assigned by this Tribunal, and Mr. Pitron is your co-counsel. And that is the situation. General Talic may stand up at any given moment and protest to this Trial Chamber that he is not represented by the counsel that have been assigned to him, irrespective of how much your assistant Ms. Fauveau is capable of defending him. That was not ever in question. It was made very clear to General Talic during last week. And this Trial Chamber commended all the efforts that were made by Ms. Fauveau in defending your client. She did excellently, given the circumstances. But still this Trial Chamber is making it very clear, you have responsibilities according to the brief that has been given to you by this Tribunal, and it is the responsibility also of this Trial Chamber to see to it that General Talic is defended in accordance with what has been provided as defence facilities for him by this Tribunal. And that, I suppose, brings the matter to an end. I demand that in future, whatever the cause you say - and I have no reason to doubt it that you had a personal medical reason which kept you away from this Trial Chamber last week. The thing is it could happen to everyone - but a simple note or a simple communication via the Registry to this Trial Chamber would have made things easier and we would have appreciated as a sign of courtesy, something I insisted upon on the very first day of this trial. Thank you. You may sit down now. So before we start with the first witness, are there any preliminaries that -- or house management procedural matters that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of the collection of documents which is called the Banja Luka collection, which is the first four binders that Your Honours have, in accordance with what was stated last week, my colleagues from the Defence, Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Fauveau, have provided to the Prosecution a List of Documents which are in dispute, which are objected to. Mr. Mazhar Inayat, the police officer who if you'll recall last week gave evidence in respect of the origin of documents in the Donia collection is waiting outside to give evidence in respect of these documents. But I've made a suggestion to Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Fauveau that perhaps a more efficient way of dealing with this is if it is dealt with at the Status Conference on Wednesday, because we are simply addressing the question of whether these documents are admissible into evidence, the first question, and the test that Your Honour laid down last week, which is for -- essentially for the Prosecution to identify the origin of the document. Now, we can call in Mr. Inayat to do that in respect of 70 or 80 documents, but we're going to be here most of the morning doing that, so we can either deal with it at the Status Conference on Wednesday, in front of Mr. Von Heble, and he can report to the Trial Chamber and then you can be satisfied yourselves on the origin of the documents. Or we can simply provide Your Honours with a list of the documents, identify on that list those that the Defence object to, you can see in our explanation column where the documents come from, and then you can decide whether or not there is sufficient provenance to accept that they are admissible. That does not in any way affect, obviously, the objections that Mr. Ackerman or Ms. Fauveau have to these documents. It is simply a question of immediate admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what is your reaction to Mr. Cayley's practical suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, which one would you prefer to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think maybe there's even an easier way. We have -- I think the Trial Chamber may not have it -- I think maybe you do have it -- a list of these Banja Luka documents that has on it the identification of the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which was the sole purpose of the testimony of Mr. Inayat last week, to tell us what that source was. We now have that on the documents, so there's, in my mind, no need for Mr. Inayat to sit here and tell what you say the document says. We can read it ourselves much quicker than he can talk about it. We have objected to the authenticity of a fairly small number of the documents, when looking at the total amount, of documents as we did before that do not have a stamp and a signature and on occasion for some other reasons we're concerned about the source of some of the documents, even though there is a -- an identified source. We're not convinced that that source is reliable. For instance, documents that come from those sources that are adversaries to our clients, may not be totally reliable sources, so we're concerned about that. It seems to me that now that you have been given in writing all the information that Mr. Inayat would have given you had he testified, that all that's left to be done is for you to look at the documents that we are suggesting should not be admitted because of their lack of authenticity and make the same kind of decision that you made last week with regard to them, whether or not you will allow them to come before you in spite of our authenticity objections. That will save both talking about them at the Status Conference and all of us sitting here listening to Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would still -- it would still require, according to me, the presence of Mr. Inayat to at least confirm the correctness and completeness of the document itself. In other words, that we would still insist upon and -- even for the tranquility of our minds, if it is a document which purports to shed information on the possible source and also reliability and authenticity of documents, at least he should confirm the totality and the completeness of the basic list, basic document. And I would suppose you would agree to that, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. I mean, my understanding from the previous practice is that as far as admission is concerned, all Your Honours require is some offering by the Prosecution on where this document actually comes from. The question of authenticity, which is linked to the probative value of the document, is of course a matter that you will consider further in your deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the thing, before I give the floor to Mr. de Roux, now, having put our cards on the table last week, and I did what I did precisely on purpose, to show you how it would go if we chose one way and once chosen that way what other possible ways were open to us, which would definitely have saved us a lot of time and which would have been much more practical than the one we opted for. As it is, the end result of that experiment is that we now have adopted a system whereby we have a list of all the documents together with the description of the source, which has already prompted, at least from the Defence of Mr. Brdjanin, a response indicating which documents are objected to. I will now ask Mr. de Roux, obviously, to see what is the reaction of the Defence for General Talic. If it is more or less the same, then the part open to us is very simple. With regard to the documents that are not being contested, the confirmation upon a solemn declaration by Mr. Inayat en bloc of all those documents would be sufficient, and he doesn't have to go, as he did last week, through each and every one of these documents and say this was -- he would be confirming the totality of those documents en bloc. As far as the others are concerned, then he would also be asked to confirm what is indicated in the basic document with the basic right of the Defence to put to Mr. Inayat any questions relating to that particular source or relating to that particular document, directed questions that are solely directed towards establishing on a prime facie basis and initially whether there is a sufficient indicia of reliability on which this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, can move ahead. So I think on this understanding, I can now ask Mr. de Roux for his comments. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I agree completely with what my colleague Ackerman said, and I think -- and I understand the Court's reasons. I think there are two problems concerning the documents. First of all, there are documents which haven't been signed, which haven't been authenticated by General Talic, which might bear his name, his typewritten name, but his signature isn't there. Then there are documents, the source of which could, in the Defence's view, be a priori suspect. These were the documents which were provided afterwards by the authorities in Sarajevo. We are perfectly well aware how in a conflict of this nature information or disinformation could be disseminated. So the documents that come from adverse sources are obviously documents for us which are not reliable, not very reliable. As far as the block of documents for which there is no discussion, I totally understand the Court's reason, and I don't see any reason for not admitting them en bloc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But still the whole point is this: that in order for this exercise to have sense and provide us with at least a terrain on which we can move with relative ease and smoothly and expeditiously, the Prosecution and more so -- even more so this Trial Chamber would require from both of you - I understand Mr. Ackerman has already done this - a clear indication as to which documents are being contested. If you leave it open, as you did last week, saying, "All documents which do not bear the signature of my client or which are purported to be his" -- at the end of the day what happened last week was that there were some of these documents which a priori had been excluded by you as being obviously not authentic and non-reliable and which, in the course of the pleadings and in the course of the evidence, had that objection withdrawn. I mean -- so what I would recommend is, first, that this matter, if you are in agreement, will be brought up, dealt with in Wednesday's Status Conference. That is my suggestion which I take from what Mr. Cayley has himself suggested. And I will stop here for a moment and ask both Defence teams if you are agreeable to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just interrupt you for a moment. In fact, the Defence counsel for General Talic have provided us with a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. de Roux has been very helpful indeed on this matter. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies if I -- I was not informed of that. So whatever I said is retracted, and we can move ahead from there. Would Wednesday's Status Conference be, according to you, the ideal forum where this matter will be threshed. I'm using a very colloquial term, but it will be discussed, debated between you, in the presence of the Senior Legal Officer. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fine. Two things. The Trial Chamber should know that the counsel for General Talic and I worked together through these documents so that we would have a joint document to provide the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second thing is that, yes, we can handle this Wednesday in the Status Conference. I'm wondering if -- the Chamber has indicated, in any event, they wanted to hear some testimony from Mr. Inayat. I'm wondering how you might want that to occur and when we might do that. Beyond that, I'm agreeable with doing it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, to put it to you very simply, we will go through the list ourselves, particularly addressing our attention to the documents that have been objected. Initially, I wouldn't expect us to waste much time going through the other documents if they are not objected to because eventually these will be the subject of our attention later on in due course when it's needed. We will have a close look, on a prima facie basis, at these documents, take stock of the substance of your objection - and when I say "your," it's also of General Talic's defence - see the nature of the indication of the information that is forthcoming from the face of the document itself and from Mr. Inayat's list. If it's the case of addressing some questions to Mr. Inayat, then of course this Tribunal will work in that direction. If it's not, we'll leave it at that. I mean, I will ask Mr. Inayat to confirm the list en bloc, and of course reserving to you, both Defence teams, the right to cross-examine him on any documents that you deem necessary. I mean, this option is -- not option, this is a right which will never -- you will never be deprived of. So you may rest assured that Mr. Inayat would still be required to come here, honour us with his presence and give some evidence with the understanding that from -- I don't know what the Prosecution will do, but from the Trial Chamber's point of view, there will be very little questions asked, if any, but you will always have the right to cross-examine Mr. Inayat on any documents that you are objecting to or disputing. Mr. de Roux. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] That's fine, Mr. President. I think that this is a matter of proceeding, which is all right. I agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose it's all right with you as well, Mr. Cayley. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's perfect, Mr. President. In a sense, from what you've said, I don't know whether there is any purpose in dealing with it at the Status Conference, because Mr. Inayat will have to give evidence for the reasons that you have already stated, so -- but I think that can be done later in the week, because this next witness is not going to be -- my understanding he's not going to be referring to any documents which are in that particular collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That actually was going to be my first question to you this morning after I asked whether there were any preliminaries. Over the weekend, I read all the statements made by this witness that had been made available to me, and particularly with the most recent of these statements, the ones that refer to the interviews that took place between the 26th and the 29th of August, but also in previous statements. There is an almost continuous reference to some basic documents. They have your, I would say, ERN number or your -- I don't know. They have a reference number, which for this Trial Chamber, over the weekend with the basic documents being here and not in our respective residences, is very difficult to follow. So perhaps you could enlighten us on this issue. Which documents are these, whether they have already been admitted in evidence on the legal basis explained to you earlier on this week, or whether these are documents which will be exhibited by the witness himself and which, therefore, will need to be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll let Mr. Koumjian explain with precision since it's his witness, but my understanding is that these are documents that the witness himself will exhibit in the proceedings, but I'll let Mr. Koumjian speak to you on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose before I give your colleague the floor that they have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: They have been, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will find out the date for you, but they will have been disclosed with the witness statements. But I will get a date on that for you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, yes, you have the floor. Thank you. Put the microphone on, please. I think it's off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the documents I planned to use in the direct examination, which is a very small amount of the documents referred to in the statements, I believe most of those were documents either obtained directly from Mr. Krzic, the witness, or documents which he will testify to having either written or seen or faxed himself, because some of these were faxed to the Bosnian embassy in Washington or the Bosnian mission at the United Nations in New York. There are, though, a couple of other documents I see on the list that I planned to use during the direct examination, two of those, and those would be disclosure numbers -- I do have the disclosure numbers for those. That's 4.1237 and 4.2139. They were part of the Banja Luka collection. I believe these were taken from the -- they're reports written from the security section. And the another document is a newspaper article which was disclosed under document 5.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, are these documents -- and Mr. de Roux, are these documents in your possession and readily available?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, after a great deal of effort, yes, we were able to find the documents. The problem was that the list given us by the Prosecutor only refers to the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I mean, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And neither one of us filed the documents using those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my problem as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the disclosure numbers would have been a much easier way for us to find them, but fortunately we, with a great deal of effort at least at my office we were finally able to located each of them and get them in a binder. So I think we have them all now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] It's exactly the same problem which the Defence of General Talic has to face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the next question that I wanted to address to the Prosecution is that in this witness's statement, particularly the most recent of these statements, there is a reference to his book. And he refers as he goes along in his statement to various passages from this book by page and also by phrases. The Chamber is not in possession of this book. I wonder what your reaction to this -- to this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution did translate a portion of this book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the book was written in Serbo-Croat. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In B/C/S, yes. And I believe 81 -- 82 pages have been translated. If Your Honours would appreciate that, we can give a copy of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the Defence been supplied with a copy of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. They were all part -- this document, the book, was a part of disclosure 7.99, which was a disclosure on this witness, I think it's called. I see it -- on my copy it's labelled "Attachment 2." And the other documents -- and I apologise if - I guess it's a lesson learned from me - if I didn't provide those disclosure numbers to counsel. I believe all the other documents were also under disclosure number 7.99. They may have attachment numbers which I didn't include in the list provide to the Defence. But I've learned my lesson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you have spoken the words I wished to say. Curiously enough, the witness refers to his own testimonies, and the documents are testimonies that refer to a book that he wrote, and we haven't got the entire copy, the integral copy, which is quite strange. And we would like to have the book in its totality be given to us because the book itself relies on other documents which we could not use the system of indirect evidence because the testimony relies on the book, and we would like to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the book was published. I don't know how available it is now. I don't have a copy of the entire book, but I know the witness does. We could possibly get a photocopy in B/C/S. This is, to my knowledge, the first time that at least I have heard of the request from the Defence for the entire book. And obviously, a translation of that at this moment is not going to be possible. But we have translated and disclosed quite a while ago the first 82 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is not asking you to translate the book. And you have confirmed that you have translated the parts from the book that the witness obviously will be make reference to. The thing is this: That last week, precisely, we had a witness who was -- referred to a book written by two historians or experts on the situation in -- on what happened in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. And he was asked on parts, specific parts, from that book. The question arose then whether that book should be available. And in actual fact, in the course of the re-examination by the Prosecution, further parts from that book, further extracts, actually, almost an entire chapter, was photocopied from that book, brought forward, and re-examination was based on the rest of that book. So more or less now I think you should, Mr. Koumjian you should know why I brought this up. It may well be important for the Defence to go through the rest of that book, just as your colleague Mr. Cayley did, in regard to the other book that we used during Dr. Donia's evidence last week. So let's not make an issue out of it. If it is possible to have in the course of the day someone photocopy this book, please do give it. The Tribunal itself does not need a copy in B/C/S, which is a language that we don't understand. But at least it should be in the records of this particular case. It should be there. And that would be the copy that the Prosecution would have provided the Tribunal with. As far as our personal needs are concerned, it's going to be of very little use, except, of course, if we need to have it here and someone will be translating bits and piece of it, which I don't think will be the case. But I think that brings the matter to an end, and we can move from there. So Mr. Cayley, shall we call your -- the witness does not enjoy or has not asked for any protective measures. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can proceed by asking the Registry to bring in Mr. Muharem Krzic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe your microphone might be on and we might be hearing your conference. At least I was hearing you. You probably didn't mean for me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, you're going to be asked to make a solemn declaration by the registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krzic, before the process of questioning commences, I would like to just give you some basic information. We are the three Judges composing this Trial Chamber. To your right is the team of the Prosecution -- for the Prosecution. And the first person, the one nearest to you will be the counsel that will be directing questions to you in chief. To your left, there are two rows. The first row consists of the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. At the back, there is the Defence team for General Talic. The accused are --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I ask that the Trial Chamber not identify the accused, since this could become an issue with regard to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And here right in front of us is the team composing the Registry. Now, you will be asked questions first by the Prosecution and afterwards by the Defence on cross-examination. I would imagine that this process will last a few days. If at any given moment you feel tired or you need a break, please do not hesitate to request -- request it from the Trial Chamber. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, just to remind you -- I know that we've spoken of this before, but I know that you speak enough English that you're going to understand most of the questions I ask in English. I remind you to wait for the translation and to pause after you've heard the entire translation just a moment, a few seconds, and then to give your answer entirely in your own language. Thank you. Sir, during the period of this indictment, which is April the 1st to December the 31st of 1992, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I lived in Banja Luka, in the area of Hijseta [phoen]. This is the part going towards Jajace, about 2 and a half kilometres from the town centre. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Sir, during this period of time, were you the president of the political party the SDA in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Koumjian was probably not here when you talked about leading questions. That was pretty dramatically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is harmless. I mean, if the question would have been do you have -- were you engaged in political activity, in what capacity, and the answer would have been just the same. You know, I mean, so I will admit that direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I'm just pointing out that he wasn't here when you set the ground rules regarding that and may not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But from his pronunciation, I understand he comes from a jurisdiction where he knows very well what a direct question is and how he should avoid it. But this is a direct question that could be admitted. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I did read the transcript of Your Honour's advice and also noted Your Honour indicated that there would be exceptions on matters to expedite the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, during this time period, did you work to promote a particular vision for your country, a political future for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was one of the founders of the SDA in Banja Luka. I was the first secretary and the first president elected by secret ballot at the end of 1991. I -- through my political activity, I tried to promote political ideas and the political statutory provisions of my party. But these political determinants were with the normal positions of law, democratic law, from all points of view and human rights. So I'm glad to say that in that respect, our political views were in compliance with general human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During that period of time, did you work to support or oppose the policies of the authorities in Banja Luka at that time, those being members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: In the first period, the period of democratic change following the fall of communism, the informal downfall, I would say, because the political parties took part in the elections, the left wing parties participated in the elections, in B and H political parties were reflected in three parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, the parties that had some joint aspirations. And there was no reason, given the democratic aspirations, there was no reasons for them not to be supported by all. I'm speaking about the early period when there was general consensus in respect of the democratic options within the frameworks of B and H as a republic and then as a state, an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't make myself clear. But this question is now dealing with the period of the conflict. And I will go back in a little while to the pre-conflict period. During the period of the conflict from April through the end of 1992, this period of the conflict, did you work at that time to oppose the authorities in power in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Could you -- well, I didn't quite understand at the beginning what you were asking me, but now I understand the question. Not only in that period but also in earlier periods, we were in a situation where we had to oppose the generally publicised views of the SDS party. The positions of that party were in collusion not only with the agreement that we had signed between coalition partners, but it was also at odds with overall human democratic legal principles in many of their segments. Of course we had to be critical towards these views and then to oppose them. As time went by, the positions in the case of the SDS party, they became increasingly centred on single-minded -- the SDS single mindedness that took no account of not only the coalition agreements but did not take into account or consideration any other political views and options. Of course I can explain this further, but I think it would be enough for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell the Trial Chamber now some of the methods that you used during this time period to oppose the authorities in power in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Well, basically and principally, we opposed the views in a political fashion, political action, in other words, public political action, action within society, through the media, through the press, by writing, action within the parliament of the municipality of Banja Luka, and action within the parliament of the Assembly of B and H through our representative. This was basically political resistance, very clear, transparent, and based on arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that part of your methods were contact with outsiders, including the media. Was that limited to media within your country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or did you also meet with foreigners?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Of course, our predominant contact were with the domestic media, the media from the former Yugoslavia, because their representatives were present in Banja Luka. But as the political and security situation exacerbated, there was never greater presence of foreign correspondents, representatives of the foreign media. And the whole relationship, attitude towards the foreign media was natural. We were very present in this campaign. And the domestic mass media were under the influence of the SDS. So we were unable to openly state our views without being corrected. I forgot to say through this, in our political activities and through our opposition and resistance, a very important activity of ours was geared to foreign representatives, representatives of the European Community who were present in Banja Luka for a period of time. These were contacts also with foreign diplomats and representatives of foreign states, American senators, for instance, and representatives of different embassies. Through these contacts, I must also mention the co-presidents of the Security Council, Mr. Owen and Mr. Vance. And as regards the position in Banja Luka, and more broadly speaking, which I will explain later on, were aimed at informing the world of the situation that prevailed in that area and with our positions in regard to that situation. In other words, we were to some extent forced to have our information reach the world, the democratic world, and in that sense we established all sorts of contacts, in writing also, with the outside world, representatives of the UN, and of different foreign embassies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to informing the world about what was going on, you mentioned the word "resistance." Did your resistance efforts also include clandestinely providing information that would be of assistance to your government about events in Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As regards what I've told you about the contacts that we had with foreign media and foreign representatives constituted also another form of process, a normal process which came into existence with the overall democratisation process in the former Yugoslavia, including Banja Luka and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So throughout that period of time before and after the elections, there was no specific need to hide such contacts or talks Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or to try and represent them in any other way to the foreign media. But we did begin at one in -- point in time to hide information. And the reason for that was the security situation in Banja Luka. At one point in time, that is on the 4th of April, 1992, Banja Luka was occupied and any resistance towards the regime was life threatening and very dangerous, especially for prominent members of political parties. Therefore, we were forced to find appropriate ways to present the information about what was going on and what we were doing about it and to have this information reach foreign media and foreign representatives, because at the same time there was a very strong propaganda by the SDS party which endeavoured to hide and conceal the terror that was going on at the time or to misinterpret it, misrepresent it, and explain it through some other means and to ignore other political parties, including their views and positions, because at the time, those positions were actually reflected by us who were representatives of our electorate. As for the ways we tried to present various types of information, I can speak about that at length if you're interested in details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you proceed. It's a very useful piece of advice that this Trial Chamber is duty-bound to give you as a witness, is that in the course of the examination-in-chief and also in the course of any cross-examination, should you be asked any questions which would entail, if you give a proper answer to them, would entail that you might be exposing yourself to criminal proceedings either in your own country or elsewhere, you are at liberty to ask the Trial Chamber not to answer those questions. In other words, in the course of your evidence, you cannot be forced in any way to make statements that may expose you to any criminal proceedings. So please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in 1996 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in 1996 did you publish a book entitled "Crimes Against the Banja Luka Krajina, 1992 to 1994"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us the year and the place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of December, 1940, in Maglaj, Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Islam is my religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what your education was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Let me start with high school, which I completed in Banja Luka. I obtained a degree from -- in Zagreb from the University of Zagreb. I am a veterinarian by profession. I also did my master's degree in Sarajevo, and I underwent a couple of specialisations, one of them, for example, in Denmark. So -- and that would be my educational background in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry to regress for a moment, but you indicated that you were born in Central Bosnia. When did your family move to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: My family lived in Banja Luka for a while during the Second World War, and at one point in time, we moved to Maglaj and Zavidovici. And I think it was in 1952 that we went back to Banja Luka. And I began my studies in 1959 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After completing your education, can you briefly tell the Court what your professional experience was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I spent several years as veterinarian practitioner. I started working in Maglaj after I completed my military service. And then in Banja Luka, I was an associate at the so-called reproduction centre. And then I moved to the veterinarian station in Banja Luka where, in 1975, I believe, I became the director, the chief of the centre, and I was in charge of several departments of that centre. And I was involved -- I also -- I was a lecturer at the University of Banja Luka. I had a course entitled "By Chemistry of Meat." For a couple of years I worked for the pharmacological institute in Zagreb, Pliva, and it was while I was working there that the aggression started. And then in January 1994, I started working for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, first as a Charges D'Affaires at the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in London. In October 1994, I became the head of the consulate of our mission in Oslo, and since October 2000, I have been working as an advisor at the Bosnian embassy in Washington until present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you're currently employed as a diplomat at the Bosnian embassy in Washington, DC, in the United States; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please remind me of the year, but I believe there was an earthquake sometime in the 1980s in Banja Luka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1969 and once again in 1970. There were two earthquakes in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Following one of these earthquakes, did you perform some volunteer activities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I really worked as a volunteer because the work had actually nothing to do with my profession. In those very difficult days following this disaster, I did my best to help people, to provide as much assistance as I could in my local neighbourhood and then also beyond with another group of young men. I was young at the time. And the following day, that is, after the earthquake, for example, I went to the former JNA cultural centre where there was a warehouse full of equipment such as ground sheets, blankets, and so on and so forth. Although there were still lots of aftershocks going on, we took this equipment, took this material and distributed it to those in need. And we helped the wounded reach the tents where some makeshift hospitals were located. I think it was recognised and appreciated by local authorities who contacted me after the disaster. There was another thing that was helpful and that was the fact that I owned a vehicle, a very small vehicle, which I used to transport this equipment but also to try and transport people to safe places such as yards and some other outdoor localities where it was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that some authorities -- I believe you said local authorities noticed your volunteer work. Were those members -- at that time would they have been members of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Speaking of local authorities, local organisations and personalities, everything was under the control of the Communist Party, but not only in a negative way, because in those days the Communist Party sought to find and organise people who meant something within the local community. The group who came to contact me actually consisted of war veterans from the Second World War. And after several contacts, they asked me to join the Communist Party, but at that time I did not yet become a member. However, they wanted my involvement in a number of social activities, which was quite an honour for me at the time being a young man. But I didn't in any way believe that such an involvement would be contrary to any humanistic principles, anything that I believed in. And that's indeed what happened. So these people came to my house. Actually, we were living in a tent in those days. So amidst this destruction, which to a certain extent resembled consequences of a war, it was quite an honour to be noticed by -- by someone like that. So shortly after that, they nominated me for the local deputy, the deputy in the local government. I think I was the youngest deputy at that time. I was elected through a secret ballot. There were two candidates. But it was only in the next round, in the second round, that I got the sufficient number of votes to become -- to become a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you join then the Communist Party, and if so, for what period of time were you a member?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Frankly, I cannot remember when that was. Probably several months after those events. But at any rate, while I was doing my military service, I was not yet a member of the Communist Party. I stayed with the Communist Party until 1978, 1980, I believe. When I left the party, it was not out of protest. I simply stopped attending its meetings. However, that did not affect my activity within the society. I was a very active member of the Red Cross in Banja Luka, and for a while I was also the head of the Banja Luka department of the Red Cross, the Centar 2 department. I was also the secretary of the municipal organisation of the Socialist Party, that is, the Communist Party, the Communist League. And I left the party at one point in time, and I had my reasons for that. If you're interested to -- in hearing them, I can tell you about them also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us, briefly, your reasons for leaving the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: You see, I come originally from a partisan family, and our idea of the Communist Party was that of an equitable, honest organisation, respectful of various ethnicities and religions. However, many of these things did not actually exist within the party. But on the other hand, those mistakes, those errors, were not so prominent as to affect in a major way the future of the society. But when Marsal Tito got old and when this generation who fought the Nazis during the Second World War got old, this cosmopolitan spirit within the Communist League weakened, and in my opinion, the prevailing spirit became that of Greater Yugoslav spirit. When I say that, I refer mainly to the ideas of the so-called Greater Serbia. This became very apparent in late 1970s, between 1970s and 1980s. I don't know whether the case of Banja Luka was more prominent in that respect or not. However, the overall atmosphere became rather disgusting, if I may put it that way. We started feeling this greater Serbian influence, and we were disappointed with this fact. We simply did not believe that such a thing could happen. And that was mainly the reason why I felt that I should leave the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you remain inactive in politics, inactive, during the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was inactive until the first multiparty elections took place. But even then, I would have perhaps remained inactive had it not been for the circumstances that made me become interested once again in the political reality. I realised that I was in a position to make my contribution to the democratic process in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, in a peaceful way. That was my motive, my wish. But my fellow citizens of Banja Luka also expressed their wish to have me become active once again, and that prompted me to become involved in politics once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to the 1980s, or remaining there for a moment, you indicated that you did some work for the Red Cross in Banja Luka. Was the Red Cross a multi-ethnic organisation? In other words, did all nationalities participate in it, and was the aid -- the people there that helped, did they consist of all nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross was an organisation at the level of the former Yugoslavia which had its local departments, or rather, branch offices. And by virtue of circumstances, I became a volunteer in the Centar 2 Red Cross organisation. That was the local branch of the Red Cross in Banja Luka. I participated in a number of volunteer activities, such as fund-raising during holidays or giving lectures about the Red Cross, the kind of work which is typical of the Red Cross organisation everywhere else in the world. I was awarded a golden medal at one point in time. This kind of award was given at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I was given this gold medal for my work for the local Red Cross organisation. It was a multi-ethnic organisation, I must say. Quite a few of its members were also members of the Communist League, but many of them were not. The Red Cross also counted among its members a number of religious people, and it was a very -- it was a very flexible organisation in that respect. However, when I started working at Pliva, my activities somewhat decreased, because I had to travel a lot throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the circumstances under which you became the President of the SDA in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The whole thing started rather spontaneously. Several prominent personalities came to visit Banja Luka, including people such as Muhamed Filipovic, Adil Zulfirkarpasic, who were quite famous figures, together with several others, who were viewed as very democratic persons who cared about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a specific entity, which was recognised as such within the former Yugoslavia. So those were the first encounters which led us to believe that soon Bosnia and Herzegovina would see formation of a number of political parties, democratic political parties. But we also realised as early as then that it would be quite difficult to organise a political party which would have a similar profile as the former Communist League, and people apprehended that -- that to a certain extent. Such meetings, such encounters - and I'm talking about those first encounters - were rather intellectual in their spirit. And they consisted of a number of very fruitful discussions as to what should be done, what needs to be done. And I have described them in great detail in my book. This group of people consisted of a number of different persons with different views, but no one thought that we should be divided along national or other ethnic lines in Bosnia and Herzegovina. No one ever mentioned any ethnic division in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those discussions were conducted amongst various ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But at the same time, we also realised that people started gathering along ethnic lines. When those parties were established, they were initially advocating these multi-ethnic ideas. So I happened to find myself in these events, but there were a lot of people who were not mature enough, politically speaking, and some people in general thought that I had enough experience and that I should become active politically. So that was the reason why I decided to help. I don't know whether you intend to bring this up later on, but I have to say that as far as the SDA is concerned, at the beginning it even counted a dozen or so Serbs or Croats as its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were elected the President of the SDA for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, the exact date escapes me at the moment, but I know that it was towards the end of 1991. It may have been in October. But I'm really sorry, I'm unable to tell you the exact date at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So from approximately October of 1991 until what date? How long did you remain the President of the SDA for Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Officially and legally speaking, had it not been for the aggression and the subsequent events, I was the president of the party until the next assembly was convened. I don't know exactly when that happened, but I believe that it was sometime in 1994. I don't remember the exact date. It was until that time that I was the President of the SDA. Several members of the Executive Council of the SDA in Banja Luka and some of the deputies of the SDA of Banja Luka convened a meeting in Sarajevo. And during that meeting, the leadership of the party was entrusted with a different person. Whereas in Banja Luka, after I was expelled from Banja Luka, it was Smail Djuzef who became the president of the party. And formally speaking, he remained in Banja Luka to lead the Banja Luka branch of the SDA, formally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps just one more question before the break. Mr. Krzic, you mentioned leaving Banja Luka. When was it that you left Banja Luka, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I left Banja Luka sometime in November 1993, some 20 days after my release from prison. And it was through the auspices of the UNHCR that I was able to leave Banja Luka. At that time I was injured, and I requested the permission to leave Banja Luka. However, without the assistance of the UNHCR, it would have been impossible for me to leave town. There were a lot of games surrounding my permission which would be given to me at one point in time but then revoked the week -- the following week. But finally, the vehicle that took me out was driven by Mr. Luigi Gentile, who was the officer in charge of the UNHCR in Banja Luka at the time, and he actually transported me to Zagreb in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will break for 20 minutes, resuming the sitting at ten to 11.00. In the meantime, the witness will remain, of course, in the same position. We will continue -- we will continue your evidence after the hearing is resumed. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Bring the witness in again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is on his way in, I would just like to inform the Court that I was informed by the always efficient Ms. Richterova, one of our trial counsels, that the book of Dr. Krzic was disclosed to the Defence in its entirety in B/C/S on the 20th of April of last year, and we also provided counsel with another copy today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We never contended it wasn't supplied in B/C/S. It's the English translation that hasn't been supplied. And as a statement of the witness, the Rules tend to require that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I mean, let's be sensible. If we were to expect that every book that a witness will be referring to which is in Serbo-Croat or B/C/S needs to be translated, even if there is one page that is going to be referred to during a testimony, I mean, you will not have the Trial Chamber behind you in that, definitely not. So where is the witness? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly was not requesting, suggesting that any book that he refers to needs to be completely translated. I was only talking about his own writings. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come that when it's the case. Mr. Krzic, you're going to continue giving evidence upon the same solemn declaration that you entered at the beginning of this morning's session. Yes, Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, we talked about Banja Luka, and I'd like you to briefly provide the Judges of this Trial Chamber a little background about that municipality. When you say you're President of Banja Luka, do you mean the city or municipality? President of the SDA. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Of course I mean the municipality. Would you like me to give you a description, provide more information? I haven't understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Banja Luka is the name of both the municipality and a city --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Banja Luka is the name of both a municipality and a city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you the President of the SDA for the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I was. The municipality of Banja Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Judges what the municipality of Banja Luka consisted of? Were there many cities? Were there villages? Just a brief description of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Apart from the urban centre itself in Banja Luka, which represented a compact part of the town, it had within its municipality tens of villages. And it should be pointed out that the Banja Luka municipality was one of the most extensive territorial municipalities in the former Yugoslavia. There were about ten villages there. I don't know the exact number, but perhaps it exceeded 50. It also had -- if we are talking about villages, it exceeded 50, but it also had local communes, village local communes, and these local communes are smaller municipal units of self-management, if I am expressing myself correctly, which was -- which were also territorial units which encompassed -- encompassed or could encompass one or several villages depending on the size. The local commune Ivanjska, Brozani Majdan were particularly prominent in this sense. Misin Han, Karanovic, and others. But the local communes also existed within the city, the town itself. We spoke about parts of the town, but these parts, these areas, also had their social and political communities, as they're called. So the municipality is at a higher level of these associations. Local communes are a lower organisational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how the various nationalities were mixed within the municipality were mixed and if there was a difference between mixing of nationalities within the city and outlying villages?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka is -- the municipality of Banja Luka is a multinational one; it always has been. But the internal distribution of the population underwent greater or lesser modifications. The greatest changes occurred from turmoje [phoen]. How do you say that in English? Such as wars -- turmoils, such as wars. Banja Luka underwent certain national changes, especially when we are speaking about the city, the town, which had always had a majority Bosnian population, Bosniak population. This majority gradually waned through wars and also because of the weather and because of earthquakes; in 1969, for example. Furthermore, the distribution of the population, the structure in the town was also influenced by the formation of a military base in Banja Luka, which I think was the biggest or one of the biggest ones in the former Yugoslavia, because with this military base -- many officers came because of this military base. There were several thousand men with their families, and we knew that the composition of this Banja Luka corps was -- it was composed of a single nationality. Banja Luka is multinational. The city is multinational. But we must say that certain areas were predominantly populated by one or another nation, by one or another people. It is characteristic of Banja Luka that the village population tended to be Serb; they were members of the Serbian population. There were fewer Croats. And there were very few Bosniaks in the village areas; we are talking about four or five villages at the most. However -- I'm thinking about the communist regime. The relation between the people -- the peoples was not that marked in society. It was not that visible. Conflicts between the peoples up until a certain time, until the influence of the old communist sector waned, these conflicts were not noticeable. Any violation of relations between people were punished, quite severely. The activity of our political parties and of the SDA, we functioned in such an environment. Banja Luka had about -- the municipality of Banja Luka, about 180, 190,000 people. I believe that you are aware of the census of 1991. And if you would like to see what the relation was prior to that date, then the census will support what I have just been saying. It's true there were certain -- it was noticed that when great changes took place, caused in this case by an earthquake, in such events, there was a -- there were slight national modifications, disturbances. People would come to Banja Luka. They were attracted to the city by the financial conditions there, the finances for the reconstruction of the city. This also -- this does not only involve reconstruction but also the extension of the city and the establishment of industry. So the arrival of people into an urban surroundings entailed certain changes, which took place among the population of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could ask you -- I appreciate all of the information you provide, but if you can try to limit your answers to the shortest answer possible to give a complete answer to the question, and then if we need additional information, we will ask you for additional questions. Can you tell us, sir, whether Banja Luka had any importance in the region as an industrial or educational centre.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Of course. By the nature of things, Banja Luka has always had its importance, historical and economic, political importance, within the new communist Yugoslavia. It was very strong in economic terms. And it was -- it had a very strong educational influence. Though it was a university centre, it had about ten departments, some of which were very important, such as the medical faculty. In addition, Banja Luka had very strong industry and very varied industry which was developing, and it created many new jobs. So as a result, it became a centre which attracted the work force or the intellectuals. Students in Banja Luka who studied there, they had greater -- better possibilities of finding employment. So some people from other republics, not just Bosnia-Herzegovina, tried to find employment in Banja Luka, and they succeeded in doing this. As a result, Banja Luka really became a fluctuating -- a changing economic and political and cultural centre in that part of Bosanska Krajina. Bosanska Krajina was often mixed in a narrow and in a -- in a more -- in a larger sense. I'm talking about this larger sense. So it was a natural economic centre, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In 1990, did you have an illness that forced you to leave Banja Luka for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Just before the elections, I had to have an operation, to leave for an operation. I went to Belgrade, and I was absent for almost a month, I think, so that I wasn't a candidate for the representative post, for the post of deputies, at no level whatsoever. I returned from this hospitalisation when the elections had actually started, so I was able to observe these elections and participate in the control of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Following the elections, can you give us a brief list of the positions that you held within the SDA party in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I was the first secretary of the party, elected at the first elections -- in the first elections. I was then elected as one of the deputy presidents. The elections were held within the -- one of the main committees of the party because it was necessary to replace the first leader, Hamza Mujagic -- Dr. Hamza Mujagic who led the party at a certain -- when there was a certain political conflict between the MBO party and the SDA. He moved -- he transferred to the MBO party. And in that vacuum, we had to find a replacement very rapidly. And when these changes were taking place, I was one of the deputy presidents of the party until 1991 -- the end of 1991, when I was elected as president of the party. I was also a member of the regional committee of the SDA party for the Bosanska Krajina region. I was a member -- I was also a member of the Main Committee of the SDA, of the SDA central branch, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the MBO party. Was that the party founded by Mr. Muhamed Filipovic, who you had mentioned earlier was involved in early discussions of the political life in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Filipovic was one of the founders, and I think that Zulfikarpasic was, too. I mentioned both of them earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What were the results of the elections in 1990 in the Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Around 90 -- 48 per cent went to the Serbian Democratic Party. The Party of Democratic Action -- these are approximate figures, so please forgive me if they're not precise. You probably have the right figures. The Party of Democratic Action about 12 per cent, 30 per cent for the HDZ. I think it was about 20 per cent for the parties on the left or perhaps a little more. I include the Reformist Party as one of the leftist parties and the Socialist Party, and I include the Liberal Party too. So the municipality of Banja Luka had about 133 deputies in total. So the SDS party did not have a majority, did not have more deputies, more than half of the deputies. In fact, the number of votes for the SDS was more or less -- was close to the number, according to the -- reflected the census of 1991 in the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the number of seats that the SDS party held in the municipality following the election? You indicated that there were 133 seats in the Municipal Assembly. Do you recall how many of those seats were held by SDS candidates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment, sir, because I see you've pulled out, I believe, a copy of your book, and we haven't talked about that. If you need to refer to anything during your testimony to refresh your recollection, I'm not sure of the Court's procedures, and I'm just going to go -- I'll ask the Court what the Court's procedures are, but I believe first you have to indicate that you need to do that and then we would ask the Court's permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've put it exactly as I was about to put it, not knowing exactly what the witness had in front of him because I can only see up to his tie and a book I couldn't catch a glimpse of. Yes. But, Mr. Krzic, before you make reference to a document, you're supposed to make that request, and you also should make available that document for anyone to see it so requesting. So will you tell us what that document you have in your hand is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for this omission, for not following your procedure. Earlier on, I told the Prosecutor that because of the extensive nature of the material or the information that you have to use when examining, and in particular when a cross-examination is taking place, I have to use documents. In this case, I have chosen my book which I wrote and for which I had full information on the truth. It's impossible to have all this information in one's head, and I would appreciate it if you could allow me to occasionally make use of the book for the sake of this information. And I'm also taking this opportunity to ask you whether I could keep my personal information with me, if I can put it here. It's just three pages from a notebook of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krzic. You don't need to apologise, because this has not been taken by the Trial Chamber as something out of disrespect or anything like that. I understand that you're not a legal man and, therefore, this has got nothing to do with courtesy or whatever. We will certainly, at this point in time, allow you to make reference to your book, because as you said, people who are walking encyclopedias are very rare nowadays, particularly in regard to events that happened in a time of turmoil like in this case. As regards the other document, if you are going to make reference to your own personal notes, then you may be requested to let us have a copy of them as you go along and prior to your being questioned thereupon. But if you're going to make reference to personal papers that you have, please make them available to both the Prosecution and the Defence. Otherwise, you have full permission from the Trial Chamber to make reference to whatever documents you require to refresh your memory or to make, put you in a position where you can give a better answer to the questions put to you or better, give us better information. Is that clear to both Prosecution and Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will only say that when -- when I was asking Mr. Donia about passages from a book, I provided the Prosecutor with copies of all those passages that I was going to ask him to refer to to enable them to follow it and to enable Dr. Donia to follow it. I'll say again, we do not -- we only have the B/C/S version and a partial English translation, and I don't know how I can cross-examine him about a book that I can't look at, and that's the problem. But I have no objection to his referring to his book as long as there will come a time when, for purposes of cross-examination, I will have it in English translation so I can cross-examine him in a fair and just manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. There are two points that have been made. One is the book, and a book, I take it from declaration and affirmation made earlier by the Prosecution, that this book in its entirety was disclosed to you in April of last year. So as far as I am concerned, the book was available to you. It was a book written by one of the witnesses that had been indicated to you, and as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, more or less that represents a closed episode. With regard to the other personal papers that the witness came prepared with, then obviously the Trial Chamber was not aware of that, of this, you were not aware of that, and I suppose that none of us is in a position to know what those documents contain, these personal papers. So the position there is definitely different. In other words, if the witness is going to ask permission to refresh his memory or to aid himself in providing us with proper answers to the questions put to him by referring to his own personal notes, then the Trial Chamber will give him the opportunity to do so provided he makes those notes available to all of us, because obviously you have a right to have a look at all those notes, Prosecution has to right to look at all those notes, and although, as I put it, none of us three knows B/C/S, we would still require to have a copy of those personal notes entered into the records. So that is the position. But as far as the book is concerned, I would imagine that Mr. Krzic is going to take days in giving evidence. You have this book. I'm sorry, I'm not going to open any further chapters there. Disclosure is there to make -- to put you in a position to be able to conduct the examination or cross-examination as it may be required, but I can't tolerate that you come here April -- so that's seven, eight -- eight months after that this document has been disclosed telling me, "I have not read it because it's in B/C/S." It was disclosed in a language, definitely, which your client understands, and you have your Serbo-Croat members of your team as well. And I would definitely not go beyond what I have already stated. We have to go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must make a proper record. If it is the position of Your Honour that I should have translated that book myself, I must advise you that the Registry will not pay for anybody to translate a book of that nature for me. They will tell me that I must submit it to CLSS. In addition, the Rules of this Tribunal require that any statement by a witness, any prior statement by a witness that the Prosecution -- a witness whom the Prosecution intends to call, the Prosecution has an obligation under the Rules to provide a translation of any statement in a working language of this Tribunal. That has not been done with regard to this book. Now, I won't know, I won't have any idea until sometime later in the next day or two what pages of this book this witness is going to refer to. I won't know whether those pages have been translated or not. We have, I think they told me this morning, 82 pages of the book that have been translated, which leaves a certain number of -- a significant number of pages that have not. And until I know which pages he's referring to, I cannot possibly know to prepare for cross-examination with regard to those pages. And once I know, if I don't have them in translation, I won't be able to read them. The Rules are violated by the Prosecution not giving us a translation of that document. Now, I understand that that is because everything is backed up in the translation section of this Tribunal. And I sympathise with that. And I'm not saying the Prosecutor should have gotten it to us any quicker. I know there's a problem with translation. I'm just telling you that it's impossible for me to properly cross-examine a witness on a book that I can't read. And so I've made my record. And I know what your ruling is. And we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, Prosecution earlier on declared that the relevant parts referred to in Mr. Krzic's previous statements and to which Mr. Krzic will be referring from in his book during at the time the present testimony had been translated and made available. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And telling the Trial Chamber that you don't know which pages from his book he will be referring to or has referred to in prior statements is not correct. I have the statements that has been made by the witness as a result -- or during the interviews of the 10th and 14th of December, 2000 and then 10th, and 12th, and 14th, and 15th of February, 2001.
