In this document, he goes through the book not exactly page by page, but he makes specific reference and specific references not only to the page number but also to the specific paragraphs that he was being asked to comment upon. That's page 18, page 21, page 24. The moment you are in a position to confirm to me that these pages have not been translated into English and not made available to you, then I will entertain further objections from you but not until then. Yes, Mr. de Roux. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I fully agree with this Honourable Chamber's position. However, I wish to note that when the witness wants to refresh his memory, opens his notebook on relevant portions or pages which have not been translated or disclosed by the Prosecution, we never know exactly which page is being used for this purpose. Personally, I don't see any bad faith in this; however, from the procedural point of view, I think that we are somewhat beyond the scope of the relevant provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to Mr. de Roux's point, I believe it would be fair that the witness cites the page that he is referring to when he does need to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Briefly, the Prosecution's position on Mr. Ackerman's points are that we do not believe that every book or article or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. every writing of a witness constitutes a statement according to the Rules. The book in B/C/S was provided nine months ago. And to my knowledge - I could be incorrect - this is the first time we have heard a complaint that the entire book should have been translated. I don't know if the Defence could have -- I believe they could have submitted it to CLSS for translation. And I would just like to point out that unlike both Defence counsel who have both B/C/S speakers next to them, I have the tremendous disadvantage of having Mr. Cayley sitting next to me who can't help me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Imagine if you had Ms. Korner too. That would have made confusion more confused. Anyway, we'll come to that. Mr. de Roux, if at any given point the witness will refer to a page from the book that I have reason to believe has not been translated and disclosed to you, then obviously the position might change according to the importance of the question and the information being sought. But we'll play it by the ear as we go along. But the position definitely at the present moment is that please don't talk to the Trial Chamber any more about having the entire book translated at this point in time and made available before any one of you feels confident in going ahead with the cross-examination. Let's be reasonable and sensible, and everyone will have his or her piece of cake. Yes. Mr. Koumjian, please proceed with your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, just to remind you of the question, which we may have all forgotten, the question was: If you recall, first, or have you refreshed your recollection through your book as to the number of seats in the municipality which were held by the SDS following the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were 65 deputies from the SDS, 14 from the HDZ, 13 from the SDA, 13 SDP, 22 SRS - this was another left wing party - and 2 from the Liberal party. I can say, perhaps, that my memory is not 100 per cent fresh, but you have official information from the electoral bodies of Banja Luka or of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if you allow me, Mr. Prosecutor - I don't know if this is allowed - I would like to turn your attention to some information. These are not -- this is not special information. There are -- it is a three-page document of decisions reflecting information from documents which I tried to summarise and which I can submit to the Defence. It is a book and refers to the book that they have received, not information outside the frameworks of the book. And not to have to turn all the pages of the books, I wanted to have this all -- all this information in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer to the question. I think we need to clarify perhaps the additional information you provided. Normally I'd ask you to just limit your answer to the question, but I will digress for a moment. Are you talking about notes that you prepared over the weekend to refresh your recollection and prepare for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And would you have any problem with providing both the Defence and the Prosecution a copy of those notes, allowing us to photocopy those?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: No problems at all. But I apologise. It is handwritten, very small writing, but I think it is legible. I think the main point of these notes is to know which page in the book we are referring to for a certain quotation, for a certain document, so that I can open it straight away and read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's very understandable, and we appreciate you organising yourself in preparation for the testimony. I would just ask you in relation to your last question -- to the last answer that you gave regarding the number of seats in the municipality assembly, did you refer to your book and, if so, which page did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I have the book before me, but I'm not referring to it. I have in fact -- I would like to mention that in the book the figures are somewhat different. I'm speaking from memory. The figures are different in regard to the overall number of deputies. In the book, it is perhaps less, one or two deputies less. So I'm speaking from memory. I think my memory is more accurate than that which has been written in the book because there may have been some typing mistakes, printing errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just for the record, which page of the book do those numbers appear on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Page 25. Page 25 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Has there only been one edition of that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, His Honour's question is: Was there more than one edition published?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Only one edition exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Prosecution, please speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Following the election, did you follow the events in the municipal assembly and the debates on various political issues that took place in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Occasionally -- yes, at the beginning, more frequently. And as time went on, less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you present ever when a debate took place regarding changing the municipal statute, as far as the number of votes that would be necessary to make changes in the statute?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. I remember that session very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had there been some debate about having Banja Luka join a group of municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina, forming an association? I believe it was called the association of Bosnia Krajina or the acronym ZOBK.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. Do I -- can I refer to my three-page document of notes, or do I have to wait for it to be photocopied first before referring to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, before this Chamber gives a decision on what has just been requested by the witness, would you request to have the photocopy of this document in your hand before he starts? Mr. de Roux? Mr. Koumjian, then you can go ahead, but when we have a break in about three-quarters of an hour's time, please make sure that this is photocopied and made available to all parties and the Trial Chamber. In the meantime, you can go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You may refer to those notes to answer the question if it would refresh your recollection to do so, but I would ask you also to close your book for now, and if you need to look at the book later, just let us know. But if you need to refer to the notes now, you may take them out, if you have them with you, and refer to the notes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As regards your question, I don't think I need accuracy in terms of the dates. I don't have to use my notes. I will speak from memory. What the atmosphere was like, I would like to describe the atmosphere at the assembly of the session. First, the rules of procedure were at discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to bring up that point myself, actually. Mr. Krzic, you have been asked a very specific question, namely, whether from your recollection the municipality of Banja Luka had been asked or whether a decision was taken to have the municipality join the association of municipalities of Bosnia Krajina, Bosanska Krajina, referred to by the acronym ZOBK. That was the question. If you know the answer, please give us the answer. And if you want to give an explanation, we will consider what you have to say, but please first try to answer that question before we go ahead with a description of the atmosphere and the circumstances surrounding at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The municipality of Banja Luka adopted that decision in an illegal fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain the process that took place regarding that decision?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It was necessary, first of all, to respect the statute of the municipality of Banja Luka. I'm not a legal expert. I don't have the statute before me. I'm speaking from memory. For every important decision of an interest, of a broader interest to the municipality, it was necessary to be adopted on the basis of a two-third majority vote. The second thing which was important at the time decisions were made that the decisions of a concern, of a broader concern for the municipality, needed to have the agreement of the coalition partners. In this case, there had to be an agreement between the HDZ, the SDA, and the peoples, in other words, that they represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That was according to the agreement between the three parties, the HDZ, the SDA, and SDS prior to 1990 elections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If the statute required a two-thirds vote to make a decision such as joining an association of municipalities, was there some effort made to change that statute, and if so, can you explain to us what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: At the assembly, as part of the agenda, a point of the agenda was a change of the statute. I think this was in May, in the month of May in 1991. And as part of the agenda, the first item was a change of the statute, because -- so as to be able to vote in favour of the proposal which was also on the agenda. However, in order to change this statute, what was lacking were the formal pre-conditions. For the changes in the statute to be carried out, a public discussion was necessary at the municipal level. That is, all the local communes had to be -- take part in this. And once a positive reply was obtained from the local centres, it was possible to formally and legally discuss changes of the statute at the level of the Banja Luka municipality. I'm not a lawyer, but as far as I know, in addition to this, the Republic Assembly, or the government through the Republic Assembly, also was duty-bound, on the basis of the then-constitution of B and H, to give its consent for every demand for a territorial change either of a municipality or of several municipalities in that sense. The very process of changing the Constitution, of attempting to change the Constitution in the municipality of Banja Luka, was carried out with a very, very loud support by the SDS representatives in the assembly. The hall of the assembly of the municipality was crowded with people who did not represent the elected deputies. There were representatives of different institutions present. And in that general confusion that entailed, it was not possible to control the voting procedure. And moreover, in this very atmosphere of coercion, voting for the statute was in fact denied by the SDA and the HDZ representatives. They left the assembly and the two left-wing parties, the SDP and the SRS remained so as to try to take off from the agenda the question of joining this ZOBK. And when they were not successful in this, they also abandoned the assembly. All that remained was a number of deputies from of the left-wing parties who were of Serb ethnicity, and according our information, along with other members of the SDS party voted in favour of a change of the statute. So that the changes of the statute, if at all they were legal, because according to our information there was no -- not even in that case even a two-thirds majority vote in favour, was in fact forced. We noted, at the time when voting took place regarding the agenda, that in -- that even those who were not representatives of the municipal assembly took part in the voting, and I think that some of the deputies will remember names and spoke these names, pointing to the people who raised their hands and who were not a part of the representative bodies in the assembly. So voting took place under pressure, no account taken of the protests and the objections of the official representatives of the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you to try to keep your answers a bit shorter. It just makes it easier for these proceedings to go forward. To summarise the information that you gave, to make sure we understand, would it be correct to say that the SDS did not have the two-thirds vote necessary to change the statute in order to join the ZOBK?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But a vote took place to change the statue. You feel it was done through improper means. And after that, the SDA and other political parties walked out of the assembly and did not participate in the municipal assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I explained the reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to move on to the period of 1991 and the war that was taking place in Croatia, and I hope you can provide the Trial Chamber with some information about how these events affected life in Banja Luka. Can you tell us what effects the war in Croatia had upon everyday life and the political situation in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict in Croatia, which at the time did not have the characteristics of a war, I was -- had the opportunity to travel through Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I can personally describe how events evolved, even from that particular angle. As the situation escalated in Croatia, in the military sense and in the political sense in respect of the conflict, in all areas in the -- the tensions in the municipality of Banja Luka were raised, being raised in an artificial way. That conflict, in fact, was a conflict between Yugoslavia and the separatists, and that atmosphere --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll just ask you not to go into the events in Croatia, but again I'm concentrating on the effect in Banja Luka. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, it became increasingly noticeable that the situation was worsening. As the situation escalated, the conflict escalated in Croatia. This could be seen in the streets with the presence of an increasing number of uniformed persons, of semi-uniformed persons. There were weapons of all kinds that moved through the streets. And their behaviour was worse every day. When I say "worse," I basically -- I'm referring to the endangerment of non-Serbs. One began singing Chetnik -- so-called Chetnik songs, and such songs were sung in front of the post office building in the city centre. Can I quote some of these songs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: "If it is necessary, from here wolves are howling. Move away, Turks, from here to Tehran. There won't be any Muslims left." In the streets, members of the Bosniak ethnicity, especially people from the villages who wore clothing, national clothing, were no longer allowed to wear this. This also referred -- this was also the case of the Catholics. And then people began wearing the clothes that Serbs usually wore. There were only slight differences in apparel, especially in the villages. On the radio, you could no longer hear Bosnian songs. A Catholic song or a Bosniak song or even songs from the Serbian milieu that were sung in Bosnia, songs glorifying the beauty of Bosnia. What we heard, that this was forbidden to be broadcast on the radio. There were different plays on the radio where one of the -- all three nations were mentioned together. It was also prohibited. In the press, one could increasingly read that the Bosniaks and the Croats represented a danger for the Serbs, not quoting what sort of danger it was, very often speaking of what had happened in World War II but describing this in a different manner. Once again the monument to the fallen soldiers in the village of Drakulici was destroyed. It is there where retaliation took place in the Second World War and about 200 people were killed. But this was inaugurated once again with representatives of the municipality, representatives of the church. Many people were present only of the Serb nationality. So the monument was in fact re-inaugurated. But in any case, there were threats of death. And then also non-Serb workers were being dismissed from factories, saying that this was a case of redundancy. Also, directors, managers, non-Serbs were being dismissed, foremen in factories in significant enterprises but also in enterprises of a military nature. And enterprises which rated with the other republics, with Slovenia and Croatia. They were prevented from working outside of Banja Luka. Their produce was looted. Their offices were seized. In the schools, gradually teachers were instructed to speak the Ekavica way of speaking and use the Cyrillic script. This was -- became an official order. And when conflict broke out in Croatia, refugees would come and tensions were rising. And it was also stated that in the educational system, teachers had to be -- that when being employed, the Serbs had priority from Serbs coming from Croatia, and Bosnians who refused to write in the Cyrillic script were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was a state of emergency declared in the city of Banja Luka by the mayor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Attempts were being made to declare a state of emergency in Banja Luka; however, we publicly opposed such attempts. Our president was Mesud Islamovic at that time, the president of the SDA, and he publicly condemned the proclamation of the state of emergency, which was contrary to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, a state of emergency can be declared only at the level of the republic. So we opposed those attempts. In media, Islamovic waged serious battle against such attempts. We were afraid of this state of emergency because we were perfectly aware of the consequences thereof. The explanation was not the increased tension in the city, the tension that I have spoken about, but the fact that Croatia was likely to attack Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the same request was made in respect of eight other municipalities apart from Banja Luka, and we believed that there was no reason for such measures. May I be allowed to put my notes on the desk, please, because I would then be able to provide you with specific dates in relation to what you're just asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, permission granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But I would say, Mr. Krzic, at this point I don't need any specific dates, so I'll move on to the next question. If you need for the next question to refer to the notes, then you may do so. Were there orders for the mobilisation of soldiers in the area at this time during the war in Croatia, mobilisation for the then-JNA, the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mobilisation was publicly proclaimed on several occasions, maybe five or six. First it was declared in respect of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Territorial Defence, despite the fact that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not issue an official approval for mobilisation, which again, we opposed publicly in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did many Muslim and Croats refuse to -- the orders for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a better way of putting it would be that they avoided receipt of such call-up papers they were hiding, because if you refuse orders for mobilisation, there are some legal consequences for that. However, several units publicly refused call-up papers. In particular, I'm referring to a unit which was composed mainly of Croat nationals. This unit was immediately officially charged by the military prosecutor for having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what were the reasons that Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka avoided the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The main reason was the fact that we all knew that such an act was illegal and was in contravention of the decisions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Second, no one was particularly eager to fight Croats. Up until that time, we all considered ourselves as brothers, and we simply couldn't understand the reasons why blood should be shed amongst us, in particular in view of what Bosnia-Herzegovina experienced during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were any measures taken against those who avoided mobilisation or against the families of those who avoided mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I have mentioned one of such measures, but there were others as well, one of them being, for example, public opposition in the media, public resistance in the media, and then, for example, various types of activities undertaken within public companies. If search papers were refused, call-up papers were refused, employees would be sacked within five days. Then there were people who were living abroad, who did not respond to the call-up papers simply by not coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This overall refusal of mobilisation brought us into a rather awkward situation because we did not have adequate papers which would have enabled us freedom of movement around the town. Without such papers, you and your family would be brought in the situation of being second-rate citizens. There were other measures as well, which perhaps are not worth mentioning at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there any retaliation against family members of those that avoided mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Retaliation followed very soon. Such families were the first ones to be exposed to what followed and to what preceded the so-called ethnic cleansing. It was those families that were first forced to abandon their property, to relinquish their property to Serbs. If a member of such a family should lose an official identification paper, they were denied a new one. And you know what it means to be without adequate identification papers in those times. If such individuals were found in the street, they would be immediately arrested and taken to the front lines, in particular, the front lines around the area of Orasje and Brcko to dig trenches there. Some of them never returned. As regards the police, when they were asked to sign a loyalty pledge, those who had refused mobilisation were dismissed. And there were many such cases within the Banja Luka SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At the end of February in 1992, a referendum was organised throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina on independence for the republic. Can you tell us about the vote in -- within Banja Luka municipality and whether or not many individuals participated in voting on that referendum.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I was authorised to conduct the referendum in Banja Luka, as far as its organisation was concerned. The authorisation had been confirmed at a meeting of all political parties except for the SDS. The SDS issued a ban on the Serb population to take part on the referendum on independence for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And one of the commanding officers of the Banja Luka barracks or maybe the staff - I'm not sure - sent a request to the media containing specific instructions as to how the ballot should read, what should be the wording of the question. In view of such circumstances, it was very difficult for the entire population to take part in the referendum. Technically speaking, and as far as the organisation is concerned, it was not particularly difficult to organise the referendum in Banja Luka. It is true that we did not have all the equipment we needed, but there were no obstructions whatsoever to count the votes. However, there was constant propaganda against referendum going on in the media. The referendum itself was conducted in all relevant areas, except in the areas which were predominantly Serb, because that was not -- we were not allowed to put boxes in the areas where Serbs constituted majority. However, in the town of Banja Luka itself, quite a few Serbs took part in the referendum. We even knew personally some of the families that participated in the referendum. But when we speak of participation in the referendum -- but mere participation in the referendum on the part of the Serb community was considered to be a hostile act, as far as Serb nationalists are concerned. The voting itself was absolutely secret. And on the level of the municipality, the total -- the turnout was approximately 45 per cent, and the total number of positive responses, that is, responses in favour of an independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was 98 or 99 per cent. I'm not sure about the accurate -- the exact number. Which means that almost all those who turned out voted in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. The referendum was observed by the representatives of the European Community. They took part in the controlling process in almost every constituency. I don't know whether I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, you have. You indicated that certain nationalists opposed the participation of anyone in this referendum. Can you give some examples of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As I said, both the media and over the radio in those days broadcast opposition of the SDS and its members to the referendum. I can mention, for example, Mr. Vukic, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Brdjanin. I remember Mr. Vukic saying something threatening, something to the effect that should the result be in favour of independence that they would not accept it, that any independence can be discussed only at the level of Yugoslavia and that all disputable areas, including those which were not predominantly Serb, would not accept those results. They were also discussing about Serbs being victims, the greatest victims in the Second World War. The statements of the opposite camp were, of course, different. Yes, that would be more or less what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had the SDS organised its own referendum the previous year, in November 1991, regarding the political future of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it had. But they referred to it as "plebiscite," as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there also, similar to the political pressure that you talked about regarding participation in the referendum in February 1992, was political pressure applied by SDS leaders for individuals to vote according to the SDS platform in the plebiscite in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Do you wish me to explain in more detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: There were explicit statements made by the SDS politicians to the fact that all Serbs should turn out for the plebiscite. There was no talk about voting but only about participating in the plebiscite, with the threat that those who did not show up would suffer consequences. In particular, leading members of the Serb community. I remember a statement by Mr. Brdjanin to that effect very well. He said that several days after the voting it would be very easy for them to discover names of managers of various companies who had not turned out for the referendum and that they would be dismissed. And not only in Bosnian Krajina but throughout the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to show the witness and have distributed to counsel and the Trial Chamber a document, and this is my first attempt to do so, but I have several copies. I have four copies of the document. It's disclosure 5.25, and the ERN number is 00547222. Would Your Honours like to me to mark that in a particular manner? It's marked. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, my understanding was that any such documents you would come forward already with an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's marked with the next number after the Banja Luka collection, 448A and B. There are copies for Your Honours, for the Court. Not for Defence on the understanding that they already have the document. And again, this is not being difficult. It's simply to avoid copying things over and over and over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I also have -- may I also have the document given in the B/C/S to the witness, and that's 448B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd ask you, Mr. Krzic, to just take a moment to read this, the article that's entitled "After the Plebiscite: You Better Give Yourselves Up."

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, do you recall seeing either this article or similar articles about press conferences by Mr. Brdjanin following the plebiscite in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Not only do I recall, but I also remember responding to such articles in various interviews. And I also remember putting this article aside, putting it in the file of our party, in the files of our party. I think that in the -- in the magazine called Glas it was given greater coverage, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, perhaps you could ask him this extract here from which newspaper. It has been photocopied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, do you recognise this newspaper as being Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is at least my impression. The Glas magazine has a different layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, is Oslobodjenje, was that a newspaper published in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was published in Sarajevo but distributed throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the former Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And if you are aware -- I don't know whether you know the answer to this. Do you know what the ethnic composition of the staff of Oslobodjenje was throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I am sure that the composition of the staff was multi-ethnic, and I also think that it reflected, not through any particular directive but rather spontaneously, the census, the last census in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, it was printed in two scripts, as you can see here. This article is written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. A couple of quick matters that I'm sure Your Honours are familiar with but perhaps just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And up to the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sure Your Honours and everyone is aware of this, but can you explain the difference between the Cyrillic script and the Latin script that is used in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: They use different symbols. But since both scripts were used in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the same manner, that is, they reflected the same variant of the language, the Ekavian variant of the language, the difference was only in symbols, in actual letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Historically was the Cyrillic script associated with the eastern areas and the Latin script with western areas, in other words, the Constantinople-Rome split?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As for the eastern and western areas, the notions are relative because there were eastern areas that used Latin script as well. Montenegro, I think, and Kosovo as well. So once again it is a relative concept. But the fact remains that the Cyrillic script was most widely used by the members of the Serb community, of Serb ethnic background because of their tradition. However, I must admit that the issue was not problematic in the former Yugoslavia. One could use any script he or she wanted to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One more quick question before the break and a change of topics. You also mentioned Glas, a -- you called it a magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe Your Honours will be hearing more about that during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly, Mr. Krzic, Glas, was that a newspaper published in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Glas was published in Banja Luka, but it was also distributed in areas, in particular areas of Bosanska Krajina, of the Bosnian Krajina. So one could argue that it was a regional paper, a local paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you, Mr. Krzic. We are going to have a break of 20, 25 minutes. Now we will resume at five to one, and you will continue your evidence then. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. The witness, please. A question: Have the notes been photocopied and circulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, they have not. We didn't obtain them from the witness yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that was the agreement. The whole agreement was as soon as he finishes, he hands in the papers, they are photocopied and made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought it would be at the break today. But he's not going to finish his direct today. But I didn't realise it was at this break. We could have easily have done it. But my mistake. If Your Honour wants, I could actually have them sent out of the courtroom now and photocopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay with the two Defence teams that we go ahead?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's okay. I was hoping we could have them before we leave today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So did I. No. We will make sure that you have them before you leave here today. In other words, at some point in time when the witness finishes his testimony for this morning or for this afternoon, then we will -- we will stop if necessary five minutes earlier, and we will have them photocopied. How many pages are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that I won't be using these notes today, so that I suggest that you photocopy them tomorrow. And as far as the book is concerned, we have agreed -- we are agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I'm directing your attention in the following questions to the period of the indictment in this case, which is from April through December of 1992. And you have indicated that you lived in Banja Luka during that time. And I want to ask you about how various aspects of life were affected -- aspects of life for the non-Serb population within Banja Luka. Sir, were there any restrictions upon the movements of those who were not of Serb nationality in Banja Luka during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about a fairly extensive time period. So some of the things that I will be mentioning here relate to the beginning and some will relate to the end of this period. There were significant changes. Significant changes occurred in the attitude toward the non-Serbian population. Above all, there were psychological changes which were very significant. All of a sudden the non-Serbian population felt like second-class citizens, and very soon a feeling developed that we were slaves or detainees in a concentration camp. So this attitude worsened, this attitude towards the non-Serbian population. The reason for this, severalfold. First of all, the reasons we can cite amount to the terror that was carried out throughout the term, the mass terror that was spread in the town of Banja Luka and which was carried out by official institutions and, of course, by non-official or paramilitary groups. That's the first reason. So some of us whose children had left because the circumstances were such -- they had gone to Sarajevo back in 1991. They went there to study -- because of the psychological pressure, we were very happy they were in Sarajevo, where the risk of mass wounding was far greater -- mass wounding and of being killed was far greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was: Were there restrictions on the movements of non-Serbs during this period of time? This answer has nothing to do with that question. And I think the witness should be restricted to the questions that are being asked him, rather than making these long narrative statements of anything he feels like talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Witness, please -- Mr. Krzic, please, you have heard the objection and the terms of that objection with which the Trial Chamber fully agrees. Please restrain yourself to answering the question and nothing but the question. Otherwise, we will go into dialogues, if not monologues, and this could be counter-productive, and it could also disrupt the pattern of questions that the Prosecutor may have prepared for you, as I am sure will be appreciated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I have to admit that this reply came to me. I'll try and answer the question as precisely as I can. Believe me, this was my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krzic. Before we move on, perhaps you could now hand over the notes that you referred to earlier so that I can have someone actually photocopying and have them prepared for counsel before the end of the day. Do you have those notes with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As I said, I apologise again. These notes really weren't intended for public distribution. I was thinking of copying them out again this evening to make them more legible. I wouldn't want such notes to be handed out because they were written rapidly and the handwriting is not very legible. I wouldn't like to make them public for this reason alone. I have certain professional duties. I'd like to prepare them a bit if I can. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the Court will correct me if I'm wrong, but these are not to be distributed publicly, but counsel for the Defence is entitled to inspect notes that you refer to, and they will respect your privacy. They will use them only for purposes of preparing their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position as explained by Mr. Koumjian is precisely the one which will be followed, Mr. Krzic. The thing is that this is a procedural matter that has to be strictly adhered to, especially as things have developed now. I don't think there is an option. These are the documents that you mentioned earlier and to which some reference has, as I understand it, has already been made, and, therefore, I kindly request you to make them available. And all -- I'm sure you're dealing with lawyers here who have a full sense of responsibility, and they will certainly not resort to any abus de confiance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe the witness is indicating, if I understood his hand gestures, that the very first page that is clipped together is not part of his notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: But all the remaining pages that within the clip are part of your notes that you prepared for this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I clipped them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back then to my question, and I'll try to make it more precise for you, regarding the period of the indictment, which is April through December 1992, I understand that that is a long period and for some of the questions you will have to explain changes that took place during this period. I want to go through various aspects of life that were affected for the non-Serb population. The first area of life I'm talking about, I'd like you to respond to, regards restrictions on movements of non-Serbs. Were non-Serbs allowed, permitted to drive their cars, to go about their business in the normal way that they had prior to the conflict after April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My specific answer is naturally no. There were various restrictions on movement. First of all, it was not possible to leave the town, except in certain extraordinary circumstances, because the risks of leaving town was increasing. And movement within town was also restricted. Checkpoints were set up, or barricades, as we would say. Very often people were maltreated at these checkpoints. Particular points in the town were isolated by using these checkpoints. These parts of towns were ones in which the majority of the population was Croat and Bosniak. And very soon cars were taken, seized by force. This took place under various pretexts and in various situations in the street. They then started requisitioning cars on a far greater scale, although cars were not requisitioned in all cases. Sometimes it was sufficient to have paid some protector, a Serbian protector, of course, and then you would keep your privileges, but you did not have the right to drive your car through town whenever you wanted to. You could keep it in the garage, and that would later give you the opportunity of travelling to Croatia with your personal belongings. Circulation was restricted in particular in the evening. Soon a curfew was imposed by the authorities, the Crisis Staff in particular and the SDS party too. These restrictions were very clear. In certain cases, the movement of the population was -- the population was almost under house arrest. I could mention a few cases in the cell Abastasi and Malhovljani, and in some occasions in Brozani and Majdan when they didn't have -- before they had to move out. This same situation occurred in other villages. Travelling to other towns was impossible because on frequent occasions people were taken off the buses when they were travelling out of town. They were sent back. They were harassed, beaten, and such passengers were often killed too. Of course the local bus network, coach network provided you with the opportunity of travelling all the time, but you risked being recognised as a Bosniak or a Croat and suffering very awkward experiences as a result. These restrictions became more and more severe as time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you yourself own an automobile during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I had two cars at the time. I wasn't able to drive either one of them. When I did so for the first time, they came to requisition it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How did you travel around Banja Luka during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I used a bike, a bicycle most often while that was possible, while people were not paying too much attentions to bicyclists, to cyclists. And in very exceptional circumstances - you could count these, the number on your -- on the fingers of your hand - I used a car until the time when they came to confiscate my car for the last time and then I wasn't able to use it any more. I often walked, of course, very often, and sometimes at night. If you asked me where and when, I could specify that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to move on to another area. You mentioned that even in the pre-conflict period the dismissals of jobs once the conflict began in Croatia. During the period of indictment, from April through December 1992, did the non-Serb population in the municipality of Banja Luka suffer from job dismissals?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I think that I have even mentioned that there were successive dismissals. The first people who were dismissed were dismissed, they were made redundant. They were said to be superfluous. But the people who were made redundant for economic reasons were also Croats and Bosnians from various companies. And then they would dismiss you for the simple reason what you are a Bosniak or a Croat. Or maybe that was the third reason. I'm not sure. It doesn't matter. And then the third pretext was that your close family members who were -- close male family members hadn't responded to the call-up. If it wasn't clear that you were loyal to the Serbian authorities, you didn't even dare go to work once the situation had escalated. So it was dangerous to go to work. It depended, naturally, on the profession, on the jobs that you had, but what is interesting that the most important professions for the survival of a population - and this relates to health workers - they were the first to be dismissed. University professors were then dismissed. It was their turn to be dismissed. At first international experts were demoted. They were no longer university lecturers or scientific experts, academic experts. They were assigned posts in the medical centre. Very soon they were not able to do that work either. Doctors were dismissed en masse, up to 25 could be dismissed in one day. I don't have the exact information or the dates. But in one period, over a thousand health workers were dismissed. Not just doctors, but health workers in general. This was the -- this was one of the worst blows to the situation of the population. Then professors at other universities who had other professions were also dismissed. Other doctors from other areas would then replace them. But they were of course of Serbian nationality. And some of them would come to work carrying arms. And you can well imagine whether it was possible for patients to visit a doctor who had a gun on his desk. These dismissals also affected the lowest classes and the highest classes, directors, for example. But they didn't stop just at dismissing people. These people were also forced to do the most menial and the most difficult jobs in the town, and it was publicly made known that the company was being -- was being shut down in Banja Luka because Bosniaks and Croats would be engaged to do this for free. So you could be a director of the greatest company in Banja Luka, and you would end up cleaning the streets. These dismissals started in the police too very soon. First of all, it affected the shifts. And especially in the state security service, replacements took place very quick. People -- the staff were replaced by Serbs. All those who were involved in monitoring foreign services were replaced by Serbs. And the ordinary policemen or technicians who refused to sign a pledge of loyalty, which included going to the front, being sent to the front, these people were replaced immediately. They lost their jobs. So the police too underwent an en masse replacement. We were informed that the situation in the army was similar, and we met many people who were from the army. I'm thinking of officers who had been dismissed because of their ethnic membership. I think that happened in the months of summer. Some were in danger because of this. As I said, I think dismissals first started because some of the teachers wouldn't accept to write in Cyrillic, in the Cyrillic script, and then this affected everyone. Only in exceptional circumstances was it possible for people to retain their jobs. For example, if they had -- if they were in mixed marriages, and the Serbian side was very much present, very strong, in such cases they might not be dismissed. But many of them had to change their names in order to keep their jobs. They had to be re-christened. It was most difficult when we're talking about this -- and this is also a form of dismissal -- when people from villages who lived from their own produce, when they were unable to bring their produce to the Banja Luka market, which used to be very well supplied -- I mention this because it's a different system of supply. So these people would individually place their products on the market in Banja Luka, not in an organised way, and this was now made impossible for them because of the numerous checkpoints surrounding the -- around the city. If a peasant turned up -- often they were women, because they were offering dairy products and vegetables. And they were prevented from going to the market and they had to find Serbian friends or to place their product or to sell it for nothing. So they were prevented from doing their work. Timbermen were also prevented from working. It was dangerous to do their work. And except in extraordinary circumstances, when they were allowed to get through because they knew people at the checkpoints, they were prevented from bringing the timber to the market, because we would buy the timber from these woodcutters at the market. At the time, it was used for heating the town. Most of the people in Banja Luka had their own heating systems. So you were unable to go and buy coal, which would be brought in by train. As a Bosniak or Croat, it was impossible to buy coal, so you had to buy wood or timber from individual producers, and you would have to pay Serbian mediators the price that they would ask for. Let's keep to dismissals. But this is also a means of denying people's right to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was the judiciary affected by the policy of discriminating on the basis of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: By all means. But I forgot to mention something. There were many veterinarians who were dismissed, regardless of the fact there were not enough Serb veterinarians. One of the local professors was dismissed -- was actually forced to resign under pressure exerted over him by his Serb colleagues. I am talking about Dr. Hodzic from the veterinarian institute in Banja Luka. As for the judges, they were all subject to numerous dismissals, and one can say that the Banja Luka municipal court and public prosecutor's office were soon rid of Croats and Bosniaks, except for some very isolated cases. But practically speaking, there were many -- there were very few Bosniaks or Croats left. The same applied to the TV, the radio, and the media in general. Very soon there were no Croat or Serb journalists left, except, once again, for some isolated cases, mostly thanks to mixed marriages or the fact that they were more loyal than it was required. Some of them were given very difficult assignments and sent to the front line. Those were able to keep their jobs to a certain extent. But those were very, very few cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one part of your last answer. The transcript as I read it of your answer is you said "Very soon there were no Croat or Serb journalists left." Is that what you intended to say, that Croat and Serbs were dismissed from the media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Croats and Bosniaks. However, any Serb who attempted to write in a different fashion would also be dismissed. I believe that one or two journalists share the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me digress for a moment, because you've raised an issue about Serbs who opposed these policies. Did you, in your activities as the SDA president and as a person who opposed the authorities in power during this time, did you find allies among some members of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, especially in 1991 and early 1992 when the situation was not so exacerbated that any contact with Serbs was dangerous. When I said a moment ago that some of the Serbs were also dismissed, I was referring to once again mixed marriages. But there were also some, so to speak, silent messages from the Serb community. One could feel that they were opposed to this new type of fascism that was going on but that they felt unable to do anything. Not only in respect of myself but other citizens of Banja Luka. They had the same impression. Some of the Serbs, and I know their names, were aware of the situation and were intelligent enough to realise that it would be dangerous even for them to continue living in this environment and left the town of Banja Luka on time and went abroad where some of them still reside. Some other Serbs offered their fellow citizens some form of protection, including myself, the kind of protection which would have exposed not only myself but them to danger as well. They offered to hide me in their apartments, which was something I couldn't accept because I wanted to remain active and public about my activities. So that was an offer I could not accept. But we received some signals, some messages from the Serb population which one could qualify as being of military or security character. Let me mention an example from my family. We had a very long-standing, friendly relationship with a rather prominent Serb family that lived in the centre of the town, and one of their members, a person the same age as me, met me one day in the street, and when he saw me, he started to cry. He was terribly upset with the situation that his people and the Bosniak people now found themselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going back to another area of life that was affected for the non-Serb population during the conflict. Was the non-Serb population, did their access to medical care, was that affected during the period of indictment, from April through December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only to a limited extent, to a limited number and in exceptional circumstances. When they were able to reach the hospital, it was through the good offices of some friends or acquaintances, and they were usually requested to conceal their real name. Access to hospital was no longer allowed to Croats and Bosniaks suffering from even most severe illnesses. They no longer enjoyed that right. And even if anyone should have allowed them to be admitted to hospital, they were very concerned because the hospital was a dangerous place because of a number of wounded soldiers that were regularly being admitted to local hospitals. It was the population in general that was seriously affected with these events. And generally speaking, one can say that they had no right to medical protection. And please don't forget that we are talking about public institutions. There were no privately owned medical institutions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of a Dr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was Dr. Vukic a prominent member of the SDS in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I think that he was the president for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of some public statements by Dr. -- excuse me. First, was Dr. Vukic -- is he a medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: He was a physician. So not a doctor by virtue of a Ph.D. He was a medical doctor, a specialist, but I'm not sure what kind. Maybe internal medicine, but again, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any statement, public statement, by Dr. Vukic regarding births in hospitals in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, with regard to this witness talking about whether or not he's aware of public statements, I object to that kind of a question being asked without some kind of prior foundation being laid, and that is: How is he aware of a public statement? Did he hear it himself, or did he hear it from someone else who heard it, or did he hear it from someone else who claimed to have heard it from someone else who claimed to have heard it from someone else? This Chamber must have some basis upon which to judge the reliability of what this witness claims to have heard and whether it came from a source that the Trial Chamber might be able to decide is reliable or unreliable. But I think for him to just start talking about things he heard, you're going to be subjected to a lot of rumour and innuendo and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you have heard the question. The question was whether he is aware of any speech that may have been made by Dr. Vukic on a particular subject. Before we can go on all the other matters that you mentioned, he has to answer that question first. Because if he is not aware, obviously all the rest doesn't come into play. If he is aware, then obviously we are going to ask him, or the Prosecution has taken the hint and will ask the witness to say how he's become aware of this speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, judging by the way he's answered questions so far, he's going to go way beyond "yes." He's going to start into one of these dialogues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, let me conduct the proceedings, because after 25 years as a Judge, I have learned to distinguish between one witness and another, witnesses that are worth stopping, lawyers that are worth interrupting. So let -- I can assure you that we will finish earlier if we continue going this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Koumjian, please. Well, I don't think you need to repeat the question. Mr. Krzic has heard it. Could you please go ahead and give us your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the record should reflect that during the dialogue between Your Honour and Defence counsel, Mr. Krzic appears to have referred to his book and to be searching through his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Krzic? You have every right to do that. I mean, no one is criticising you. It's just for record purposes and because you have a Prosecutor who is definitely searching to be loyal to his counterparts on the Defence and also with the Trial Chamber, something which is appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I realise that my testimony here is of a rather comprehensive nature and that trying to respond to questions such as this, I simply have to consult my book. One other thing, I do understand English, and I have followed the counsel for Defence, and I have in the meantime prepared my answer in light of that. And that is the reason I wanted to check this piece of information in my book, because I understood the objection. Second, I should like my notes to be given back to me, because it's very difficult for me to work without them. However, I am prepared to provide a response to the question that has just been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please go ahead and give us your answer, please. Yes. As the president of the SDS or permanent member of the Executive Council thereof, Dr. Vukic made some public statements which encroached upon -- or rather, which were tainted with anti-semetic and international aspects. I am going to tell you only three examples, because I haven't had enough time to consult my notes. Dr. Vukic had an interview on the radio, Sarajevo-aired radio, together with Mr. Hadzialijagic. The reason I wanted to refer to my notes is because I think the time frame is rather important. He spoke in a very rude manner, disrespective manner, about Bosniak -- rather, Muslim women. He insulted publicly their honour and made some very explicit threats which were addressed to Turks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, when I say "Turks," I'm talking about a very derogatory term for the Muslim community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a derogatory term which has nothing to do with the reality of their background. However, it is a very offensive term for Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the fact that he said that publicly on TV as the president of the SDS party can only be interpreted as a direct physical threat to that segment of the population. We replied to this statement. We quoted his words, and I believe that I also wrote an article which was published in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Koumjian, I have to draw your attention that we have already overstepped the time allotted --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to this Trial Chamber. So if it is convenient for you to stop your direct examination now, we will do it. If you have not more than one, two short questions, then we can proceed. But I can't guarantee a short answer to those, so I would suggest with your indulgence to stop here, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. It's understood the witness will remain in the same condition he is now, which is as a witness and with all that it entails, and that tomorrow morning he's expected to be here present so that you can proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Your Honour, we do have copies of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to check with the witness, because I see that the first page is copied with what appears to be a phone number. And if I can just show that to him. I don't believe he wanted this page to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Check it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can do that after the Court adjourns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the Court raises now, and we will resume our work tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of February, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25
